name: Marco Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm Costa's Field with my dad, who's semi-retired and still thinks he's in charge. It's 45 hectares: about 120 outdoor pigs, field vegetables, and a veg box scheme that goes out to 300 households on Thursdays. My mornings are pigs and planning, afternoons are picking and packing. I run the whole box scheme off an AI assistant now, the orders, the route, the emails when the courgettes fail. My partner Ana is a part-time nurse, and our boys, Leo and Tomas, are ten and seven.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mud and margins. The pigs churn the field to soup every winter and the supermarket price for pork hasn't moved in years. The box scheme is what keeps us afloat. I'm also trialling a little solar weeding robot from the growers' co-op, which I adore and my dad calls the Roomba.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, that would be a letdown for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, not a miracle. I'd still tell people at the growers' co-op it saves me a day a week on the box scheme admin. I'd probably post a short thread about the weeding robot being slower than promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I was hoping the robots would get good enough to take the back-breaking jobs and make small farms like ours easier to run. If it all stalls, we're stuck with the same margins and the same mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for the box scheme and push it a bit further, maybe to plan crop rotations and predict demand. I'd keep the weeder on trial and give honest feedback to the co-op. And I'd keep saving our usual 150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of disappointment. Like a promised holiday that turned into a long weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the AI actually do for you on a Thursday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI builds the delivery route around which customers are home, and it writes the 'sorry, no leeks this week' email in a way that doesn't sound like I'm crying. Last Thursday it saved me about two hours. My dad still prints the order list out on paper and checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd be pleased if it stalled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, definitely. He'd say 'told you so' about the Roomba every day for a month. Ana would be pleased too, honestly, because she thinks I spend too long fiddling with gadgets.

S0.say: Fair enough, it's a tool, not a miracle. It still saves me a day a week on the box scheme admin.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed. I was hoping robots would take the back-breaking jobs and make small farms easier to run, but we'd be stuck with the same margins and mud.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for the box scheme and stretches it to crop rotation planning and demand forecasting. Keeps the weeding robot on trial, gives feedback to the co-op and keeps saving 150 a month.
S0.quote: The AI builds the delivery route around which customers are home, and it writes the 'sorry, no leeks this week' email in a way that doesn't sound like I'm crying.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is the rare farmer who would be let down if AI stalled. He sees robots as relief from hard physical work on a small farm. His father's scepticism comes up repeatedly and seems to be part of the family humour.

steps.text: Keep the solar weeding robot on trial and give the growers' co-op honest feedback
Stretch the box scheme's AI assistant to plan crop rotations and predict demand
Keep saving the usual 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's interesting. That's more or less what I'm planning for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms have to get in early and share the kit, or the big ones will hoover up the benefit. I'd say that at the growers' co-op and online. And I'd argue for public grants so the machines aren't just for the rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could do well out of this. A couple of shared robots for weeding and pig feeding, and suddenly I've got time to grow the box scheme to 500 households. The risk is that the supermarkets get the same robots and squeeze prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put about 6,000, nearly all our savings, into a co-op share of two weeding robots and a feeding system for the pigs. I'd use AI to work out which veg earn the most per hour. And I'd try to sign up 100 more box customers before the supermarkets work out what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited, with a small knot about spending the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nearly all your savings is a big bet with a mortgage. What does Ana think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana would make me write it all down, the costs, the worst case, what we'd do if the robots broke. We'd agree to keep one month's money back no matter what. My partner Ana is the brake and I'm the accelerator, and that's why the farm still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our seasonal pickers, mostly. We hire four people every summer, and two of them have come back for eight years. I'd want to keep them on packing and deliveries, but I can't promise that.

S1.say: Small farms have to get in early and share the kit, or the big ones will take all the benefit. There should be public grants so the machines aren't just for the rich.
S1.think: I could do well out of this, with shared robots giving me time to grow the box scheme to 500 households. The risk is that supermarkets get the same robots and squeeze prices.
S1.do: Puts about 6,000 of savings into a co-op share of two weeding robots and a pig feeding system, keeping one month's money back. Uses AI to rank crops by earnings per hour and tries to sign up 100 more box customers.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, with a knot about spending savings.
S1.quote: My partner Ana is the brake and I'm the accelerator, and that's why the farm still exists.
S1.fieldNote: Marco sees steady disruption as an opportunity and would move his savings into shared robots fast. His partner acts as a check on risk. He worries more about his seasonal pickers than about himself.

steps.text: Put about 6,000, nearly all the savings, into a co-op robot share, keeping one month back
Bring two shared weeding robots and a pig feeding system onto the farm
Use AI to work out which vegetables earn the most per hour
Argue at the growers' co-op that small farms must share the kit early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's not a farming timescale, that's barely two harvests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for public ownership, or at least public shares, in AI and robots. If machines do almost all the work, the gains have to come back to people. I'd be out campaigning for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the robots don't scare me. My customers losing their jobs does. Box schemes run on teachers and nurses and office workers paying a bit extra for good veg, and if they lose their incomes, my business goes with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the box scheme expansion straight away and hold onto our cash. I'd automate as much of the farm as I could on co-op loans, so our costs fall as fast as prices do. I'd join the campaign for an AI dividend, and I'd start selling meat and veg at the weekly market in town as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the farm work, but for who's left to buy the food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo and Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody knows what jobs will look like, so they should learn to grow things and fix things and talk to people. Leo already helps me with the weeder app. Tomas just wants to name the pigs, which honestly might be the only job left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots don't scare you. Is there any version where they do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, one. If the robots belong to three companies and we just rent them, I'm not a farmer any more, I'm a tenant in my own field. That's why the ownership fight matters more than the machines.

S2.say: This is the moment for public ownership, or at least public shares, in AI and robots. If machines do almost all the work, the gains have to come back to people.
S2.think: The robots don't scare me; my customers losing their jobs does. My box scheme runs on teachers, nurses and office workers paying extra for good veg.
S2.do: Halts the box scheme expansion and holds onto cash. Automates as much as he can on co-op loans, campaigns for an AI dividend and starts a weekly market stall in town as a backup income.
S2.feel: Anxious, not for the work but for who is left to buy food.
S2.quote: If the robots belong to three companies and we just rent them, I'm not a farmer any more, I'm a tenant in my own field.
S2.fieldNote: Marco's fear in fast AGI is demand, not technology: his customers' incomes would fall. He'd still automate but hold back on growth. Ownership of the machines matters to him more than the machines themselves.

steps.text: Automate as much of the farm as possible on co-op loans to cut costs
Join the campaign for an AI dividend paid back to everyone
Start selling pork and veg at the weekly market in town as a backup
Stop the box scheme expansion straight away and hold onto the cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. I can work with five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms and towns should be planning together now. Local food co-ops, shared robots, a fair share of the AI money for communities. I'd be pushing our council and the growers' co-op to start in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the farm could come through this in good shape. We'd automate step by step and turn the place into somewhere people visit, because in a world with lots of free time, people want to see where food comes from. My worry is still my customers' incomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd buy into the shared robots with about 4,000 and keep two months' savings. I'd start planning farm visits and school trips, maybe a pick-your-own patch, with Ana running the bookings. And I'd help the growers' co-op write a five-year plan for robot sharing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the background, but mostly up for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I lead or react. With two years I'm grabbing whatever I can and hoping. With five I can test things, make mistakes, and still be standing when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad make of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble and then he'd be the best guide on the farm visits. My dad's got sixty years of stories about pigs escaping onto the main road. Robots can't tell those.

S3.say: Farms and towns should plan together now, with local food co-ops, shared robots and a fair share of the AI money for communities. I'd push the council and the growers' co-op to start in the first year.
S3.think: The farm could come through in good shape if we automate step by step and become somewhere people visit. My worry is still my customers' incomes.
S3.do: Buys into shared robots with about 4,000 while keeping two months' savings. Starts planning farm visits, school trips and a pick-your-own patch with his partner, and helps the co-op draft a five-year robot-sharing plan.
S3.feel: Uneasy in the background, but mostly ready for it.
S3.quote: My dad's got sixty years of stories about pigs escaping onto the main road. Robots can't tell those.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Marco shifts from defence to building something new, a farm people visit. He sees time as the difference between leading and reacting. His father reappears, this time as an asset.

steps.text: Buy into the shared robots with about 4,000, keeping two months' savings
Start automating the pig and veg work step by step with the co-op robots
Plan farm visits, school trips and a pick-your-own patch, with Ana taking bookings
Help the growers' co-op write a five-year plan for sharing robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd love ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to get it right: ownership, sharing, retraining, all of it. I'd be on every panel that would have me. I'd also say it's no excuse for waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one feels good for me. Ten years is enough to automate the farm properly, build the visits side and maybe train other small farmers in how to use the robots. I think I'd end up teaching as much as farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a short course in agricultural robotics at the college, about 600, so I could teach it later. I'd keep up the shared robots and add a pig-feeding unit by year three. And we'd put 50 a month aside for each boy's training or studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and pretty hopeful, which I know sounds odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you're fine. Is there anything here you'd lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tiredness, which I won't miss, and maybe the feeling that I earn my bread with my hands. I like coming in filthy. If robots do the dirty work, I'll have to find something else to be proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything for the boys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop assuming either of them takes over the farm. If they want it, great, but I'd rather they choose it in a world where it's a nice life, not a trap.

S4.say: This is a chance to get it right: ownership, sharing, retraining, all of it. But it's no excuse for waiting.
S4.think: This one feels good for me. Ten years is enough to automate the farm properly, build the visits side and maybe teach other small farmers to use robots.
S4.do: Takes a short agricultural robotics course at the college for about 600 so he can teach it later. Keeps the shared robots, adds a pig-feeding unit by year three and saves 50 a month for each son's training.
S4.quote: I like coming in filthy. If robots do the dirty work, I'll have to find something else to be proud of.
S4.fieldNote: Marco is at his most relaxed with ten years and imagines teaching other farmers. His only loss is a sense of pride in hard physical work. He'd stop assuming his sons will take on the farm.

steps.text: Take a short agricultural robotics course at the college for about 600
Keep the shared robots and add a pig-feeding unit by year three
Put 50 a month aside for each of Leo and Tomas's training or studies
Speak on every panel that will have him about robot ownership and retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of the robots, but because my customers would lose their jobs before anyone sorted out how to share the money. What would help is a proper AI dividend paid to everyone, and cheap co-op loans so small farms can own their machines instead of renting them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who's going to buy the food. Everyone asks if farmers survive. But a farm with no customers is just a garden.

headlineQuote: A farm with no customers is just a garden.
portrait: Marco Costa, 43, runs Costa's Field, a 45-hectare pig and vegetable farm with a 300-household veg box scheme, alongside his semi-retired father. He uses AI every day and is trialling a weeding robot, and he'd be disappointed if AI stalled. He'd put savings into shared robots under steady change, and becomes anxious only when fast AGI threatens his customers' incomes. With five or ten years he plans farm visits, teaching and family education funds, and always argues for shared ownership of the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his customers would lose their incomes before anyone worked out how to share the gains.
whatWouldHelp: An AI dividend paid to everyone, and cheap co-op loans so small farms can own their machines rather than rent them.
